citation.title: Changing Climates of Conflict: A Social Network Experiment in 56 Schools

standing_assumptions:
The article (PNAS 113(3):566–571; printed pp. 566–571 are main PDF pp. 1–6) and its SI Appendix (43 pages; the printed page number equals the supplement PDF page number) state no theorem, proposition or lemma and give no proof. Their formal objects are the school-level regressions (SI Eqs. (1)–(6)), the exposure mapping, the exposure probabilities and the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator (SI pp. 16–19), one sentence of asymptotic justification (SI p. 19) and the notes to Tables S6 and S7. There are two official corrections: PNAS 115(15):E3598 (2018), which replaces 30% by 25%, and a 2019 correction that adds a grant number. Everything quoted below was read from the rendered page images.
(S1) Schools and blocks. SI p. 5 (Study design): “Prior to randomization, schools agreed to participate in all measurement aspects of the program, with a 50% chance of receiving the anti-conflict program (the treatment).” “Schools were assigned to blocks of four, and randomized to receive the treatment or not within these blocks.” “Four schools dropped out from the study before the point of randomization, which left the total sample at 56 schools and 24,191 students.” Fig. S1, caption (SI p. 24): “The 56 schools were first blocked into groups of four by pretreatment school level variables including size and student demographics (see SI). Within each of the 14 school blocks, two schools were assigned to control (the two school networks on the left), and two to treatment, the anti-conflict intervention (the two school networks on the right). The nodes depict the population of students at the school. Grey nodes are the “seed eligible” students, selected by a deterministic algorithm and comprising a representative sample of the school. Seed eligibles were blocked into four equally sized groups based on pretreatment characteristics including gender and grade, and half of the students in each block were randomly assigned to be treated (part of the anti-conflict program) if they were in a treatment school; dark green nodes are treated seed eligibles. Nodes in the shape of stars are the social referents, who are in the top 10% of their school in connections reported by other students in the pre-randomization survey.”
(S2) Seed-eligibles and seeds. SI p. 6, with $a_i$ a student's indegree and $b_i$ the student's closure: “The students in each of the gender-grade-$b_i$ blocks with the largest values of $a_i$ were considered eligible for randomization into the seed group, such that we had no fewer than 40 seed-eligible students (schools with fewer than 200 students), and no more than 64 seed-eligible students (schools with less than 550 students). For schools with between 200 and 550, we scaled linearly between 40 and 64 seed-eligible students, rounding to the nearest 4. Table S2 demonstrates the covariate profiles of eligible and ineligible students. All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups. Among treated schools, half of the seed-eligibles were block-randomized into the seed group, using 4 blocks constructed using gender, grade, and $b_i$ (using an R package, blockTools).” Main p. 567 (PDF p. 2): “In the 28 of 56 schools randomly assigned to receive the intervention, we selected a group of students (the seed-eligibles) using a deterministic algorithm (see SI Appendix for materials and methods used) designed to represent 15% of the school population, blocked by gender and grade and capped at 64 students (grades ranged from 5 to 8) (SI Appendix, Figs. S1 and S2, and Table S1). We randomly assigned 50% of that group (the seeds) to be invited to participate in the anticonflict intervention, which our team implemented over the course of the school year. Within each seed group at each school (on average 26 seeds at each school, for a total of 728 seeds across 28 schools), a random proportion were social referent seeds, meaning they were in the top 10% of their school in the number of connections reported by other students (i.e., indegree).”
(S3) School-level (climate) regressions. SI p. 13: “We fit the following linear regression model: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}$ (1) where $ij$ denotes the $i$th school in the $j$th block. $Y_{ij}$ denotes school-level outcomes, $\alpha_j$ is a block-level fixed effect, $D_{ij}$ is the school-level treatment assignment, $C_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed group (percentage of seed group that is classified as a social referent), and $C^E_{ij}$ is the composition of the seed eligible group (percentage of seed eligible group that is classified as a social referent). $\tau$ here is the average causal effect of treatment. We include $C^E_{ij}$ as a covariate control here so as to maximize comparability with the interaction model in (4). In all cases, the model is fit with OLS regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to characterize uncertainty.” The interaction model, Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), and its interpretation are transcribed in P037-T14. SI p. 16: “This amounts to fitting the following model for main effects: $Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}$, (5) where $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ is a vector of school-specific pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$).” Main p. 568 (PDF p. 3): “We computed confidence intervals and P values using robust SEs under a normal approximation.” Main p. 567: “(Administrative data were available for 49 of the 56 schools, and we restricted our attention to these schools for analyses of conflict-related events.)”
(S4) Scale of composition. In the targets $C_{ij}$ and $C^E_{ij}$ are fractions in $[0,1]$ (0.20 means 20%), the scale of Fig. 2 and Table S7. The SI's wording (“percentage”, “$c\%$”, “percentage points”) does not match that scale; this is finding P037-N020, rated a clarity note, and is not a target.
(S5) Social-influence setting. SI pp. 16–17: “We have a finite population of students indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ on which our randomized experiment is performed. Define a treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_N)'$, where $z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ denotes whether or not student $i$ is assigned to be a seed (i.e., is invited to participate in the anti-conflict group). An experimental design is a plan for randomly selecting a particular value of $\mathbf{z}$ with predetermined probability $p_{\mathbf{z}}$. Restricting our attention only to treatment assignments that can be generated by our experimental design, define $\Omega = \{\mathbf{z} : p_{\mathbf{z}} > 0\}$, so that $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$ is a random vector with support $\Omega$ and $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = p_{\mathbf{z}}$. In this setting, treatment assignment is the random assignment of seeds both across and within schools according our hierarchical randomization (i.e., so that half of schools are assigned to control schools with no seeds).” The exposure mapping $f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i)$ with $\theta_i$, $\gamma$ and $s_i$ (SI p. 17) is transcribed in P037-T7. SI p. 18: “We allow for each student $i$ to have a vector of potential outcomes, which we denote by $(y_i(d_C), ...y_i(d_D))$, that do not depend on the value of $\mathbf{Z}$. We seek estimates for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$ (i.e., control exposure, school exposure, non-social referent peer exposure, social referent peer exposure) of the average potential outcome $\mu(d_k) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i(d_k)$.” “$\pi_i(d_k) = \sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega} \mathbf{I}(f(\mathbf{z},\theta_i) = d_k)\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$.” “We restrict ourselves to the subpopulation of students (n=2451) for which there exists some probability that students could receive all four exposures: $0 < \pi_i(d_k) < 1$ for $k \in \{C, S, NI, I\}$.” The estimator $\widehat{\mu_R}(d_k)$ (SI p. 19) is transcribed in P037-T11.
(S6) None of the eleven headline claims (P037-H1 to P037-H11) is a mathematical statement: each is an empirical estimate, a description of the design or an interpretive conclusion. Every target below therefore comes from a confirmed error.
(S7) [Added on 6 October 2026, after the authors' analysis code became available; it applies to the revised P037-T2 and to P037-T18 onward.] The authors' eleven R scripts, as released by ICPSR with study 37070, were not available when (S1)–(S6) and P037-T1 to T17 were written. In the targets added or revised afterwards, ‘the released code’ means those scripts as read and run by the checkers; a statement of what the code does is established by the code and is not a statement of the publication. ‘On the public data’ means a value obtained from the public data release (ICPSR 37070 V2) run through the authors' scripts with an adapter, or from a reconstruction on that release; the authors' own analysis files are not public and ICPSR states that some variables in the release were changed, so such a value is not the value the authors would obtain from their own files. No such value is part of a target's statement: the statements are exact identities, probabilities, counts and counterexamples, and values on the public data appear only in notes, as aggregates (the data are respondent-level records of school students; no respondent row and no school identifier is given). The scripts are cited by number: script 1, ‘1. Sanitize and generate perms, probs.R’ (the network, referent status, the simulated seed and school assignments, the exposure indicators and their simulated probabilities); script 2, ‘2. Cleaning.R’ (outcomes and covariates); script 3, ‘3. Network results.R’ (the social-influence estimates and their randomization standard errors); script 4, ‘4. School results-with-correction.R’ (the school-level regressions, their three kinds of standard error, the percentages of the 2018 Correction and Fig. 2); script 6, ‘6. Bond et al analysis.R’ (Fig. S5). Line numbers are those of the released files, as cited by the checkers.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Main Methods, ‘As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group’, with SI Appendix Eq. (2) (repeated as Eq. (4)), its interpretation, and Eq. (6), as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 568 (PDF p. 3); SI Appendix pp. 13–14 and 15–16 (supplement PDF pp. 13–16); Table S7 note, SI p. 42
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 568] “To characterize effect heterogeneity with respect to the seed group composition (i.e., the proportion of seeds who are social referents, which varies from school to school), we use linear regression interacting school-level treatment with seed group composition and controlling for the proportion of students in the seed group who were social referents. Although there was heterogeneity across schools in the proportion of seed-eligible students who were social referents, any differences between the proportion of treated seeds who were referents and the proportion of seed-eligibles who were referents are attributable to randomization. As a result, our regression strategy allowed us to estimate the causal effect of the proportion of social referents in the seed group on school-wide conflict and other outcomes. Accordingly, we can make comparisons between average potential outcomes in, for example, treated schools where seed groups had 20% social referents to control schools, or even to treated schools where seed groups had 10% social referents.”
[SI pp. 13–14] “To characterize how the seed group's composition (i.e., percentage of referents) affects the efficacy of the program, we also use an interaction model.
$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + u_{ij}. \qquad (2)$$
Here, assuming that the linear approximation for causal effect heterogeneity is valid, $\tau_0$ is the average causal effect of treatment when the composition of the seed group is 0% referents and $\beta$ represents the slope of the average causal effect with respect to group composition in percentage points (i.e., assuming that the slope is constant, the average causal effect of treatment at a given composition $c\%$ is $\tau_0 + \beta c$.) As $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}] \propto C^E_{ij}$, controlling for $C^E_{ij}$ ensures that any random deviations in $C_{ij}$ from $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ may be interpreted causally. For both models, we also use pretreatment covariates (percentage white, percentage English-speaking, average house quality and, where available, pretreatment measurement of $Y_{ij}$) to improve efficiency by including them as linear controls in the regression model.”
[SI pp. 15–16] Eq. (4) repeats Eq. (2) and the two sentences that follow it (with ‘(I.e., assuming that the slope is constant, ... is $\tau_0 + \beta c$.)’ printed as a sentence of its own). “We also use covariates to adjust our interaction model:
$$Y_{ij} = \alpha_j + \tau_0D_{ij} + \beta C_{ij}D_{ij} + \gamma C^E_{ij} + \boldsymbol{\theta}\mathbf{X}_{ij} + u_{ij}. \qquad (6)$$
Interpretation of the causal effects proceed as above; inclusion of covariates is solely for efficiency improvement.”
[Table S7 note, SI p. 42] “Regression-based estimates of the effects of treatment conditional on the proportion of social referent seeds in the group, under a linear approximation.” ... “Estimates computed using ordinary least squares with covariate controls and fixed effects for randomization block. A control is also included for the expected value of the seed group composition in the school (over all possible randomizations).”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $Y_{ij}$, $\alpha_j$, $D_{ij}$, $C_{ij}$, $C^E_{ij}$, $\mathbf{X}_{ij}$ as defined on SI pp. 13 and 16 (standing assumption (S3)); the design (standing assumptions (S1), (S2)); ‘All of our estimates are computed conditional on the composition of the seed-eligible groups’ (SI p. 6). The paper does not define ‘the linear approximation for causal effect heterogeneity’, gives the school-level outcomes no potential-outcome notation, and does not say with respect to what $\mathrm{E}[C_{ij}]$ is taken (the Table S7 note: ‘over all possible randomizations’). The results that rest on this passage: Table S7 (peer conflict: $0.04$ with robust SE $0.07$; interaction $-0.85$ with robust SE $0.46$), Fig. 2 with ‘($P$ = 0.07, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test)’, the 20% projection of Results, p. 569 (P037-T13), the abstract's ‘The effect was stronger when the seed group contained more “social referent” students’ (p. 566) and the Discussion's ‘future interventions would do well to use as many social referents in their intervention group as possible’ (p. 571).
canonical_claim.note: The printed interaction interpretation expressly carries the validity qualification. The preferred reading is a conditional average causal response with sufficient residual mean or orthogonality; no universal design-alone identification claim is attributed to the paper. The interpretive passage remains not_applicable as a separate theorem.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results, first paragraph (‘the treatment significantly reduced ... ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test)’), and the last sentence of the 2018 Correction (‘remain statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level’), as printed
canonical_claim.location: main p. 569 (PDF p. 4); 2018 Correction, p. E3598 (correction PDF p. 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Main p. 569, Results] “We first turn to the question of school climate, as measured by schools' overall levels of norms and conflict behavior. Figs. 1 and 2 reveal that the treatment significantly reduced average levels of disciplinary reports of peer conflict in treatment compared with control schools ($P < 0.05$, heteroskedasticity-robust Wald test). In a control school, we estimated that each student in the school was officially disciplined for peer conflict on average 0.20 times per year. We estimated an average decrease of 0.06 disciplinary events per student in treatment schools, a 30% reduction in peer conflict reports.”
[2018 Correction, p. E3598] “The authors wish to note the following: “We reported an estimated 30% decrease in administrative reports of conflict and would like to correct this estimate to 25%. The original paper reported this estimate as the rounded covariate-adjusted estimated average treatment effect ($-0.06$) divided by the rounded unadjusted control group mean (0.20). Without the rounding error, the original estimate is 29%. Using both covariate adjusted estimates, we have an estimate of 25%. Using both unadjusted estimates, we have an estimate of 23%. The original estimate of 30% was reported in the Abstract (line 11), the Significance Statement (line 8), in the results on page 569 (left column, first paragraph, line 9), and in the discussion on page 571 (left column, first paragraph, line 6). In each of these places, we would like to replace the number 30 with 25. The estimated overall effects on administrative reports of conflict remain statistically insignificant at the $\alpha$=0.05 level.””
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The test and the estimate are those of P037-T3: the school-level main effect $\tau$ of SI Eq. (5), estimated by OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and referred to a normal approximation (main p. 568; SI p. 13); Table S6, Peer conflict: School level main effect $-0.06$, Heteroskedasticity Robust SE $(0.03)$ (SI p. 41). The Correction describes no new coefficient, standard error, test or threshold.
canonical_claim.note: Listed because finding P037-N008 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. The two sentences are empirical reports of a test, not mathematical statements; their only formal content is that, read as reports of the same test, they assert $p < \tfrac1{20}$ and $p \ge \tfrac1{20}$, which no real number satisfies (P037-T3 (i)). Lean cannot decide which sentence is wrong: Sol's falsity flags refer to the pair, and neither sentence is shown false by itself. If nothing can be stated beyond P037-T3 (i), not_applicable is the right status. The percentage in the same passages is P037-T6 and P037-T17.
